newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HORSE RACING-TRAINERS, JOCKEYS HIT IN HK SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-TRAINERS, JOCKEYS HIT IN HK SCANDAL.

text.p: Hong Kong's elite horse racing establishment was jolted on Tuesday when the Jockey Club suspended licences of two star trainers and five jockeys in a clean-up linked to one of the territory's worst racing scandals.
The development followed the court appearance of five other people charged by the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) for taking illegal bets.
On Monday the ICAC said 37 people had been detained over two days, including five jockeys, two trainers and three Jockey Club staff, but it did not identify them.
The Jockey Club said in a statement that the licences of the trainers and jockeys were suspended "to maintain the confidence of the public in the conduct of racing".

The two star trainers, at the forefront of the British colony's wildly popular horse racing scene, were Chan Pak-Hung and Leung Sik-Lun, it said. Two jockeys were Yim Hin-Keung and Choi Chun-Wai, and the other three, all apprentice jockeys, were Ho Wah-Lun, Tam Shu-Man and Ko Chun-Ho.
Licences of all seven would be suspended until April 2, or until a time determined by stewards of the club, the club said.
The Jockey Club, which has a monopoly on horse racing and gaming in the territory, has vowed to clean-up the game.

"The Hong Kong Jockey Club is determined to keep horse racing clean," Wilson Cheng, the club's information secretary, told Reuters, but added that this weekend's races would go ahead despite the turmoil caused by the race fixing inquiry.
Earlier, five people -- two Malaysian citizens and three Hong Kong residents -- were charged in a district court for bookmaking by the ICAC.
All five pleaded not guilty and were released on bail. They will appear in court again on May 16.
The charges stem from the biggest race fixing and illegal betting scandal on Hong Kong's race courses. None of the other 32 people questioned have been charged so far.
The ICAC has said it had freed on bail 19 of the people it originally detained, but the probe was far from over.
It said in a statement that those still detained would be released later on Tuesday. The ICAC cannot hold detainees longer than 48 hours without bringing charges.
The Malaysians charged were named as Yong Seng-Chen and Liew Siew-cheong. The three Hong Kong residents were Chan Hung-yip, Kam Tat-Fai and Ching Fuk-hung.
The Malaysians, both businessmen, were released on bail of HK$750,000 (US$96,200) each in cash, and the Hong Kong defendants were released on bail of HK$100,000 each (US$12,800).
A court prosecutor said the ICAC obtained evidence showing the Malaysian duo had been accepting bets, amounting to substantial sums, from Macau, Singapore, Malaysia and Gibraltor.

The races are the only legal outlet for a flutter on the horses in gambling-mad Hong Kong. Horse racing is one of the biggest businesses in the territory of 6.4 million people, outperforming some weighty blue chip companies in turnover.
Betting turnover in the 1995/96 season was HK$80 billion (US$11 billion), believed the highest per capita in the world.
